title: Strange Meeting
tagline: Wilfred Owen's powerful poem of a meeting between enemies in a strange underworld and the deep waste and sorrow of war.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material and original practice questions written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI English Literature (Paper 2) syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). 'Strange Meeting' by Wilfred Owen is named only because it is listed among the prescribed poems in the ISC Class XI prescribed texts. BoardPrep does not reproduce the text of the poem or any CISCE examination question; the explanations and practice questions here are original and are meant to support study of the prescribed poem, not to replace reading it.

overview.intro: 'Strange Meeting' is one of the five prescribed poems for ISC Class XI English Literature in RHAPSODY: A Collection of ISC Poems. It imagines a meeting in a place beyond ordinary life, where one soldier encounters the enemy he has killed, or perhaps the enemy he might have killed. The poem is remarkable for its pity rather than for glory. It presents war as a destruction not only of life but of what life might have been: the lost possibilities, the unlived future and the deep sorrow of a world fractured by violence.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: The pity of war; enemy and victim; loss of future lives; death beyond the battlefield; the waste of young lives; pity, guilt and shared suffering

learningOutcomes: Identify the unusual setting and the meeting it makes possible.
Explain why the poem is often read as an anti-war poem.
Discuss the importance of the 'enemy' figure in the poem.
Describe the sense of lost time and unlived lives.
Support observations with brief reference to the poem.

blocks.text: The poem begins with a movement into a place that is not the ordinary world. That setting matters because it gives the poem room to turn from the battlefield to something more inward and symbolic. The meeting is 'strange' not only because of the location but because of the relationship between the people involved. A soldier is meeting someone whose life has been affected by the same war, and the encounter is charged with grief rather than triumph.

items: The setting creates distance from the battlefield.
It allows the poem to think about death and loss in a deeper way.
The meeting is emotionally charged because of the shared war.
The strangeness of the place mirrors the strangeness of the situation.

items.text: A reader might expect a war poem to stay on the battlefield. This one moves away from the moment of fighting so that it can examine what war has done beyond the immediate violence.
items.note: The setting helps the poem become commemorative and reflective rather than only action-based.

blocks.text: One of the poem's most powerful effects is its treatment of the 'enemy'. In ordinary war talk, the enemy can be reduced to an opposite. Here, the figure on the other side is not simply defeated or erased; he becomes a person with grief, memory and loss. The poem quietly removes the distance between victor and defeated. In that sense, it undermines the usual enemy logic of war by showing shared suffering.

items: The poem challenges the simple division of friend and enemy.
The figure encountered is not just an opponent but a sufferer.
The meeting suggests that war creates shared loss, even across opposing sides.

items.text: A student may ask whether the poem says war is meaningless because both sides suffer. That is a fair starting point, but the poem is often more intimate than a simple moral statement: it shows one painful recognition at a deeply human level.
items.note: The poem's force comes from pity, not from abstract argument alone.

blocks.text: A striking part of the poem is its sense of what war destroys beyond death itself: the possible lives, discoveries, kindnesses and understandings that will never happen because a young life has been cut off. The poem grieves not only for what happened but for what will now never be. This gives it a feeling of waste that is deeper than a simple battlefield death count. The future itself seems to have been damaged.

items: The poem mourns lost possible lives.
It presents war as a destruction of potential.
The loss is both personal and wider than one body.
The sense of waste gives the poem its tragic weight.

items.text: A reader might focus only on the death of one soldier. A fuller reading notices the poem's larger grief: that every loss removes something that might have become part of the world's future.
items.note: The poem is tragic because it sees death as a loss of possibility.

blocks.text: The poem is often remembered for its pity. It does not celebrate courage in the old heroic way; instead, it looks at war with sorrow and anger. That does not make it soft. It makes it devastating. The language can be severe, but the overall effect is one of grief for what war has done to people and to humanity. This is why the poem continues to feel powerful: it refuses the easy language of honour without denying the reality of suffering.

items: Pity is the poem's dominant tone.
The poem refuses glory-based ideas of war.
It presents suffering as something to be mourned, not praised.
The tragedy comes from the scale of waste and the intimacy of the meeting.

items.text: A student may sometimes think anti-war poetry is only 'against war'. This poem is more than opposition; it is an attempt to feel the ruin that war leaves behind in human terms.
items.note: The poem's value lies in its compassion as much as in its protest.

keyPoints: The poem places a deeply moving meeting in an otherworldly setting.
It blurs the line between enemy and fellow sufferer.
It mourns not only death but the loss of future lives and possibilities.
Pity is more important in the poem than glory.
The war is presented as a waste that damages the future.
Brief reference to the poem supports an answer better than a general opinion about war.
examFocus: If the question asks about theme, focus on pity, loss and the human cost of war.
If the question asks about the 'meeting', explain why it is significant that it is between those affected by the same war.
A good answer notices the poem's sadness and anger without reducing it to a slogan.

vocabulary.meaning: Deep sorrow for suffering, especially when it seems unnecessary or cruel.
In the poem, a place associated with the dead or the afterlife, used to frame the meeting.
The loss or destruction of life, value or potential, especially in war.
The opposing soldier, who in the poem becomes a figure of shared grief.
A serious, sorrowful outcome, especially one involving loss and suffering.
The sense that pain and loss are experienced by people on more than one side.

questions.prompt: The dominant tone of 'Strange Meeting' is best described as:
questions.explanation: The poem is most powerful for its grief and its sense of waste.
questions.commonMistake: Reading the poem as a celebration of bravery or victory.

questions.prompt: The poem's 'meeting' is important because it:
options: Brings together people affected by the same war in a deeply human encounter
Is only a dream with no meaning
questions.answer: Brings together people affected by the same war in a deeply human encounter
questions.explanation: The meeting allows the poem to explore pity and shared loss.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the meeting as a random or purely literal event.

questions.prompt: What does the poem suggest about the idea of the 'enemy'?
questions.answer: It suggests that the enemy can also be a suffering human being with loss and grief, so the simple division between victor and defeated is weakened.
questions.explanation: The poem humanises the figure who might otherwise be reduced to an opponent.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the poem is only about one soldier's enemy in a narrow sense.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem mourn more than just the death of a single soldier?
questions.answer: Because it also mourns the possible lives, experiences and futures that will now never happen, so the loss extends beyond one body into the wider world of what might have been.
questions.explanation: The poem's sadness includes the loss of potential, not only immediate death.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the loss as only a single personal death.

questions.prompt: Discuss how 'Strange Meeting' presents war as a waste rather than a glory.
questions.answer: The poem presents war not as a noble adventure but as a source of grief, loss and ruined possibility. The meeting itself is strange because it brings together those shaped by the same conflict, and the encounter creates pity rather than pride. The poem is especially tragic when it imagines the futures that will now never exist. By refusing glory and focusing on suffering, the poem makes war feel like a destruction of human life in the deepest sense, not merely a military event. The pity of war is therefore its central message.
questions.explanation: A good answer connects setting, encounter and the sense of lost futures to show why the poem is anti-war in feeling.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the poem is against war only because it mentions death.
